filename: New Scientist Story Ideas — Autism — September 2026.md
title: New Scientist Story Ideas — Autism — September 2026

studies.title: Genetic evidence questions why autism is diagnosed so much more often in boys
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely provocative genomic result on one of autism's most familiar "facts," limited by the abstraction of GWAS-based methods.
studies.the_study: Researchers at the University of Colorado Boulder used Genomic Structural Equation Modeling on sex-stratified and age-at-diagnosis-stratified autism GWAS summary statistics, regressing them against 68 psychiatric, cognitive, health and social traits. Early- and late-diagnosed autism showed strikingly different genetic association profiles, and these differences were not explained by sex. But the genetic correlation between male and female autism was high, with few sex-specific associations — which the authors say "questions the biological basis for disproportionate prevalence rates in males." Female-diagnosed and late-diagnosed autism both correlated more strongly with internalizing traits.
studies.why_it_matters: If the common-variant genetics of autism are essentially the same in males and females, the 4:1 diagnostic sex ratio looks less like biology and more like who gets noticed, and when — with timing of diagnosis emerging as a more meaningful genetic dividing line than sex.
studies.pitch_angle: Lead on the woman diagnosed at 42 whose brother was diagnosed at 4 — and the finding that the genetics say she is not a different kind of case because she is female, but because she was spotted late. Call Sophie Breunig and Andrew Grotzinger at the Institute for Behavioral Genetics, and an autism-and-gender researcher such as Meng-Chuan Lai for a counterview on the female protective effect.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on "age at diagnosis as a biological variable" — how the late-diagnosed adult cohort may constitute a partly distinct phenomenon from childhood-diagnosed autism, and what that does to prevalence statistics and service planning. Fits a policy-facing outlet or a long-read in a science magazine's health section.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of existing GWAS summary statistics; common-variant signal only, so says nothing about rare high-impact variants; diagnostic-ascertainment effects are baked into the source data; predominantly European-ancestry samples.

studies.title: Told a listener is autistic, people don't simplify their speech after all
studies.ns_score_reason: a clean, pre-registered null that contradicts a widely reported lived experience; held back by the small sample and lab-task setting.
studies.the_study: In a pre-registered study, 33 non-autistic adults (mean age 36) gave map-route instructions to a confederate who in one condition disclosed being autistic and in the other did not. Across speech rate, syntactic complexity, semantic complexity and discourse features, there was no evidence of the simplification seen in "Elderspeak" or foreigner-directed speech. Exploratory analysis found that more positive attitudes toward autism were associated with *less* accommodation on one measure.
studies.why_it_matters: Autistic people frequently report being talked down to, but this suggests the label alone is not the trigger — something else in real interactions (behavior, pauses, atypical eye contact) may be cueing patronizing speech, which redirects where the research should look.
studies.pitch_angle: Open with the autistic adult who says strangers switch to "explaining voice" the moment they disclose — then the lab test that couldn't reproduce it. The tension between lived report and null result *is* the story. Call Vikram Shukla and Sudha Arunachalam at NYU, and Vikram Jaswal at Virginia, who works closely with autistic collaborators.
studies.wider_angle: A broader piece on speech registers as unconscious social sorting — Elderspeak in care homes, foreigner-directed speech, baby talk to wheelchair users — and the emerging evidence on when these registers help comprehension and when they simply signal low expectations. Fits a general-interest magazine or a linguistics-friendly outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (33); single confederate and a constrained Map Task rather than natural conversation; null result may reflect low power or demand characteristics; disclosure was verbal only, without the behavioral cues present in real encounters.

studies.title: More empathic autistic children fare worse when they withdraw socially
studies.ns_score_reason: large sample and a result that inverts the assumption that empathy is uniformly protective; weakened by parent-report-only measures.
studies.the_study: Parents of 689 autistic children and adolescents aged 5–17 (76% male) completed measures of shyness, unsociability and social avoidance, cognitive and affective empathy, and emotional problems. All forms of social disengagement were linked to empathizing difficulties, with social avoidance strongest. Crucially, the link between unsociability or avoidance and emotional problems was *stronger* in youth with higher empathy; shyness showed no such moderation.
studies.why_it_matters: It complicates the popular framing of empathy as a straightforward protective asset and suggests that autistic children who read others well but stay away from them may carry the highest emotional cost — a group easily missed because they look socially competent.
studies.pitch_angle: The empathic autistic teenager who chooses solitude and suffers for it. Lead on the counterintuitive interaction: empathy amplifies rather than buffers the emotional toll of withdrawal. Call Lacey Chetcuti or Mirko Uljarevic (Stanford) and Eva Loth (King's College London).
studies.wider_angle: A trend piece on the crumbling of the "autistic people lack empathy" cliché — from the double empathy problem to alexithymia research to hyper-empathy accounts — and what happens to services when the deficit story is replaced with a mismatch story. Fits a psychology-focused or health outlet.
studies.caveats: Cross-sectional and observational, so no causal claim; all measures parent-reported, including empathy; sample skewed male; concurrent, not longitudinal, emotional problems.

studies.title: Treating parents' stress lowers autistic preschoolers' emotional meltdowns
studies.journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: randomized trial data with observational coding as well as parent report; limited by being a secondary outcome analysis with no untreated control arm.
studies.the_study: Secondary analysis of a randomized trial (NCT03459625) comparing mindfulness-based stress reduction with psychoeducational support for parents of 117 autistic preschoolers. Neither the parents' mental health nor the child was the direct target of child treatment, yet parent-reported child emotion dysregulation and observed dyadic dysregulation both fell across groups, and reductions in parenting stress predicted reductions in reported child dysregulation. Children's independently observed dysregulation, measured while alone, stayed largely stable.
studies.why_it_matters: It supports the idea that a young autistic child's emotional regulation is partly a property of the parent-child pair rather than the child alone — and that intervening on the adult can shift the dyad, though not necessarily the child's solo regulation.
studies.pitch_angle: Treat the parent, help the child. Open in the post-diagnosis window, when families are most overwhelmed, and use the dissociation between dyadic and solo measures as the intellectual hook — what exactly changed? Call Rachel Fenning (Claremont McKenna) and Carla Mazefsky (Pittsburgh), developer of the Emotion Dysregulation Inventory.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on co-regulation across the lifespan — infants, autistic children, couples, dementia caregiving — and the measurement problem of deciding whether "regulation" belongs to a person or a relationship. Suits a longer psychology feature or a science podcast.
studies.caveats: Secondary analysis of a trial not powered for these outcomes; both arms were active treatments so improvement could reflect time or attention; parent-reported outcomes contributed strongly; short follow-up; N=117 across two arms.

studies.title: One in five autistic adolescents shows signs of catatonia — most often girls
studies.ns_score_reason: a striking prevalence figure in an under-studied age group with clear clinical resonance; single-clinic sampling caps it.
studies.the_study: Clinicians systematically assessed 107 autistic adolescents aged 12–20 at a tertiary psychiatry clinic in Ankara using DSM-5 criteria and the Bush-Francis Catatonia Rating Scale. Catatonia was identified in 21.5%, most commonly presenting as stereotypy, impulsivity, echolalia and verbigeration. Female sex and clinically significant separation anxiety were independent predictors; the catatonia group also scored higher on depression and stereotyped-behavior measures.
studies.why_it_matters: Catatonia in autism is thought to be routinely missed because its signs are read as "just autism," and this suggests it may be present in a substantial minority of autistic teenagers — a treatable condition hiding inside an untreatable label.
studies.pitch_angle: The autistic teenager whose sudden slowing, freezing and loss of speech was attributed to regression, and the diagnostic overshadowing that keeps catatonia invisible. Frame around the female skew, which cuts against autism's male-dominated clinical picture. Call Rahime Duygu Temelturk (Ankara University) and a catatonia-in-autism specialist such as Amitta Shah in the UK.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on catatonia's rehabilitation as a transdiagnostic syndrome — across schizophrenia, mood disorders, autism and autoimmune encephalitis — and the argument for routine screening. Fits a medical or psychiatry-focused outlet.
studies.caveats: Single-center tertiary clinic, so referral bias likely inflates prevalence; N=107; cross-sectional with no follow-up on course or treatment response; symptom overlap with autism makes rating-scale thresholds contentious; population may not generalize beyond Turkey.

studies.title: Feeling at home in your body predicts later self-esteem in autistic adults
studies.ns_score_reason: first longitudinal test in autistic adults with a decent sample and a directional finding; short follow-up and self-report limit it.
studies.the_study: 262 autistic adults in the UK (aged 19–73, mean 38) completed measures of body appreciation, self-esteem, life satisfaction and flourishing at baseline and again three months later. Cross-lagged panel modeling showed that higher baseline body appreciation predicted increases in self-esteem and flourishing — but not life satisfaction — with no reciprocal effect running the other way.
studies.why_it_matters: Body image research in autism has been almost entirely cross-sectional; a one-directional prospective effect makes body appreciation a plausible intervention target rather than just a correlate of feeling good.
studies.pitch_angle: Positive body image is usually discussed in the context of dieting and social media, rarely in autism — yet sensory differences, interoception and years of being told your body moves wrongly make it a distinctive issue. Open with an autistic adult describing stimming as bodily reclamation. Call Phaedra Longhurst and Viren Swami at Anglia Ruskin.
studies.wider_angle: A piece on interoception as the missing link between autism, body image and eating disorders — autistic people are heavily over-represented in anorexia clinics, and this line of work suggests why. Fits a health or mental health specialist outlet.
studies.caveats: Observational; entirely self-reported online measures; 3-month follow-up only; self-selected UK online sample likely skews toward late-diagnosed, verbally fluent adults; no autistic comparison group with differing support needs.

studies.title: A quarter of people with intellectual disability on multiple antipsychotics exceed the maximum recommended dose
studies.ns_score_reason: a hard, quantifiable number on a long-running scandal, but the paper is framed as a methods feasibility study.
studies.the_study: Records for 424 adults with intellectual disability prescribed two or more antipsychotics were pooled from eight specialist NHS services in England and Wales, covering 2017–2023, and doses were converted into chlorpromazine-equivalent units. Autism was recorded in 42–58% of cases and "behaviours that challenge" in 77–87%. More than 25% were on the equivalent of over 1000 mg/day of chlorpromazine, exceeding the British National Formulary maximum.
studies.why_it_matters: Despite a decade of national campaigns to stop the over-medication of people with learning disabilities and autism, there has been no way to compare prescribing burden between services; this shows it can be done — and that a quarter of a polypharmacy sample sits above the licensed ceiling.
studies.pitch_angle: A decade after England's STOMP program launched, here is the first cross-service yardstick — and it finds routine over-ceiling dosing. Open on the arithmetic problem: two "normal" doses of different antipsychotics can quietly add up to an unlicensed one. Call Rohit Shankar (Cornell/Plymouth) and Angela Hassiotis (UCL).
studies.wider_angle: An investigative piece for a UK news or health-policy outlet on whether STOMP has actually changed prescribing, using chlorpromazine equivalents as a measurable audit tool that regulators could adopt.
studies.caveats: Retrospective convenience sample of only eight services, selected for those already on ≥2 antipsychotics, so not a prevalence estimate; no clinical outcome or harm data; chlorpromazine-equivalence conversions are contested; no control for indication severity.

studies.title: Autistic adults imagining "what if" blame circumstances where others blame people
studies.ns_score_reason: an elegant eye-tracking design and a nicely specific difference, but effects are subtle and the story needs careful handling.
studies.the_study: Autistic and neurotypical adults produced counterfactual alternatives to narrative events while their eye movements were tracked in a visual world paradigm. Autistic participants were slower to begin speaking and more disfluent, but were no worse at generating counterfactuals, and both groups preferred additive counterfactuals. The difference lay in content: neurotypical adults were more strongly biased toward human causes and flexibly shifted their gaze to human agents depending on response type, while autistic adults considered physical causes more often and showed uniform gaze patterns.
studies.why_it_matters: It replaces a deficit account — autistic people struggle with counterfactual thinking — with a difference account: equal capability, different default about what could have been otherwise, which has downstream implications for blame, regret and self-recrimination.
studies.pitch_angle: "If only I'd left earlier" versus "if only the train hadn't been late" — the same event, two different regrets. Lead on the finding that autistic adults are just as good at counterfactual reasoning but reach for physical rather than human causes. Call Heather Ferguson at the University of Kent.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on counterfactual thinking as the engine of regret and blame — how the alternatives your mind reaches for first shape whom you hold responsible, in courtrooms, accident investigations and relationships. Fits a general-interest psychology feature.
studies.caveats: Sample size not stated in the abstract and likely modest; lab narrative task with uncertain real-world transfer; group difference is in bias strength, not presence; autistic adults recruited as verbally fluent adults, so results may not generalize across the spectrum.

studies.title: Autistic traits show up in how steadily you walk across campus
studies.ns_score_reason: vivid, relatable, unobtrusively measured in the real world; small N and subclinical trait design keep it modest.
studies.the_study: Ninety-three participants walked across a university campus twice, the second time with a distractor task they were told either to ignore or to attend to, while their gait dynamics were captured unobtrusively and analyzed at moment-to-moment and time-invariant levels. Higher subclinical autistic traits were associated with less stable local gait dynamics regardless of task context. Exploratory analyses suggested that instructions to ignore the distractor shifted local dynamics for social anxiety traits but global dynamics for autistic traits.
studies.why_it_matters: It shows mental-health-relevant traits leaving a measurable trace in something as mundane as walking, hinting that everyday motor behavior could be a low-burden window on cognitive style — though the effects are population-level, not diagnostic.
studies.pitch_angle: Your walk as a readout of your mind. Lead on the unobtrusive capture — no lab, no treadmill, just people crossing a campus — and be strict about the fact that this is subclinical trait variation, not a walking test for autism. Call Lynden Miles at the University of Western Australia.
studies.wider_angle: A piece on the "digital phenotyping" boom — gait, keystrokes, phone accelerometry as passive mental-health signals — and the privacy and validity problems of inferring minds from movement. Fits a technology or ethics-focused outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (93); non-clinical student-heavy sample with trait measures rather than diagnoses; key task-context findings are explicitly exploratory; cross-sectional; single-center.

studies.title: Scrolling without posting is linked to withdrawal in autistic and ADHD young adults
studies.ns_score_reason: the active/passive split is a clean hook and the transdiagnostic framing is fresh; entirely self-reported and cross-sectional.
studies.the_study: 101 UK young adults aged 18–24 with self-reported diagnoses of autism (n=52) or ADHD (n=49) completed the Hikikomori Questionnaire (HQ-25M) alongside estimates of active and passive online engagement. Total online time did not differ between groups, but autistic participants reported higher overall hikikomori vulnerability, driven by socialization difficulties and physical isolation. Across the whole sample, passive social media use correlated with withdrawal vulnerability — particularly isolation and lack of emotional support — while active use did not.
studies.why_it_matters: It shifts the question from *how long* neurodivergent young people spend online to *what they do there*, and imports the Japanese concept of hikikomori into a UK neurodevelopmental context as a continuum rather than a category.
studies.pitch_angle: Screen time isn't the variable that matters. Open on the autistic 20-year-old who spends hours watching other people's lives scroll past without ever typing anything. Call Mark Brosnan at the Centre for Applied Autism Research, University of Bath. Be explicit that causal direction is unresolved — withdrawal may drive passive use, not the reverse.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on hikikomori going global — how a concept coined for Japanese young men is being retooled as a transdiagnostic vulnerability measure in Europe, and what gets lost in the translation. Fits an anthropology-inclined or international current-affairs outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (101); self-reported diagnoses and self-estimated online time; cross-sectional so direction of effect unknown; group differences in engagement patterns described only at the level of effect sizes; narrow age band and UK-only sample.

studies.title: Autistic children's pupils reveal the extra effort of seeing things from another viewpoint
studies.journal: Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry
studies.ns_score_reason: three converging measures in a decent developmental sample; the underlying phenomenon is familiar, the mechanistic dissociation is what's new.
studies.the_study: 43 autistic and 38 neurotypical children and young people completed a visual perspective-taking task in which their own view and an avatar's were congruent or incongruent, while EEG event-related potentials and, in a subsample, pupil responses were recorded. Autistic participants were less accurate at rating the avatar's perspective and were more disrupted by incongruency, both behaviorally and in a late-frontal slow wave. Their pupils also showed larger, more sustained responses — an effect statistically dissociable from the EEG difference.
studies.why_it_matters: It suggests that difficulty taking someone else's visual perspective in autism is not purely "social" but is partly a domain-general problem with filtering out irrelevant information — and that autistic children may reach similar answers by working harder.
studies.pitch_angle: The pupil as an effort meter. Lead on the possibility that what looks like reduced perspective-taking is partly the cost of suppressing your own viewpoint — a selective attention problem wearing a social mask. Call Luca Polzer or Christine Freitag at Goethe University Frankfurt.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on effort as the hidden variable in neurodivergence — masking, compensation, and why matched task performance can conceal wildly different internal costs, with links to autistic burnout. Fits a mental health or workplace-focused outlet.
studies.caveats: Modest N with a smaller pupillometry subsample; laboratory task, not everyday perspective-taking; pupil size is sensitive to luminance and arousal confounds; no measure of downstream fatigue; single-center.

studies.title: Control for age, and autistic children's imitation looks much like everyone else's
studies.ns_score_reason: a useful corrective with eye-tracking backup; two small studies and a statistical-control argument that will be contested.
studies.the_study: Two studies compared selective imitation in young children with autism and cognitively matched typically developing children under social and nonsocial model conditions, controlling chronological age and correcting for multiple comparisons. Once chronological age was accounted for, groups performed similarly on almost all tasks, with one exception (the social "door-closed" task). Wearable eye-tracking in Study 2 found broadly comparable gaze allocation to the model's face, action area and surroundings; initial differences in face-directed attention did not survive age-controlled analysis.
studies.why_it_matters: Two headline claims about early autism — that imitation is selectively impaired and that children look less at faces during demonstrations — largely dissolve here once a basic confound is handled, which is a caution worth taking seriously across the developmental literature.
studies.pitch_angle: How much of what we "know" about autistic toddlers is an age artifact? Lead with the vanishing face-looking difference, and the broader replication problem in developmental autism research. Call Gökhan Töret at Hacettepe University, and a face-processing researcher such as Terje Falck-Ytter for pushback.
studies.wider_angle: A methods-driven feature for a research-community outlet on matching in developmental studies — mental age versus chronological age versus neither — and how the choice quietly determines which group differences appear.
studies.caveats: Sample sizes not reported in the abstract and likely small; statistical control for chronological age is not equivalent to design matching; single research group; the one surviving group difference is not explained; no follow-up.

studies.title: Autistic children's brains take a different route to reading
studies.ns_score_reason: the reversed brain-behavior correlation is genuinely surprising, but with 13 autistic children this is preliminary at best.
studies.the_study: Diffusion-weighted MRI from 25 children (13 autistic, 12 neurotypical) was used to map 16 language-related white matter tracts. Autistic children showed higher quantitative anisotropy in six tracts and higher isotropic diffusion in two, suggesting denser fiber bundles with more surrounding free water. Strikingly, the direction of the brain-reading relationship flipped between groups: in autistic children, *lower* anisotropy in the left arcuate fasciculus went with better reading comprehension, while in neurotypical children higher anisotropy did.
studies.why_it_matters: If it holds, it implies autistic readers recruit more localized pathways rather than the canonical integrated language network — meaning the same brain measure means opposite things in different groups, a warning for anyone building "biomarkers" from pooled samples.
studies.pitch_angle: The same brain signature, opposite meanings. Frame around the biomarker problem: a measure that predicts good reading in one group and poor reading in another. Open on hyperlexia, common in autism and poorly explained. Call Rajesh Kana at the University of Alabama at Birmingham.
studies.wider_angle: A skeptical feature for a neuroscience-literate outlet on the replication and sample-size crisis in diffusion MRI, using the group-by-brain interaction here as an illustration of how easily such effects arise by chance in tiny samples.
studies.caveats: Very small N (13 vs 12), described by the authors as preliminary; single scanner and site; cross-sectional; group-by-measure interactions are especially fragile at this sample size; the "biomarker" framing in the abstract runs well ahead of the evidence.

studies.title: Parents with depression stick with online parenting therapy best
studies.ns_score_reason: a nicely against-the-grain engagement finding, undercut by small N and secondary-predictor analysis.
studies.the_study: 68 parent-child dyads with neurodevelopmental diagnoses (children aged 2–6) took part in a time-limited internet-delivered Parent Child Interaction Therapy program, with attrition, homework, coded observations of parenting skills and child compliance all tracked. Parents of children with ADHD and children with better receptive language were more likely to complete. Parents who themselves had a depression diagnosis showed the *highest* completion rates and the greatest improvement in parenting practices. An autism diagnosis predicted less improvement on only one parent-reported measure and none of the observed ones.
studies.why_it_matters: Parental depression is routinely treated as a barrier to engagement in behavioral parent training; here it predicted the opposite, and autism diagnosis barely affected objectively observed outcomes — both useful correctives for who gets offered these programs.
studies.pitch_angle: The parents clinicians worry about most were the ones who finished. Lead on the assumption being overturned, then the parallel finding that autistic children did as well as anyone on observed measures even though parents *reported* less change. Call Rosmary Ros-DeMarize at the Medical University of South Carolina.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the parent-report/observation gap in child mental health trials — how much of "treatment response" is a change in the child versus a change in the parent's perception. Fits a clinical-research or evidence-focused outlet.
studies.caveats: Small N (68); predictor analysis within a single uncontrolled treatment cohort, not a randomized comparison; parental depression was diagnosis-based, not severity-graded; single center; results may reflect who self-selects into an online program.

studies.title: Latino teenagers assume they'll care for an autistic sibling; others aren't so sure
studies.ns_score_reason: an under-covered group and a clear cultural contrast, but a small qualitative study with limited generalizability.
studies.the_study: Semi-structured interviews in English with 21 non-autistic youth siblings of autistic individuals (12 Latino, 9 non-Latino), aged 8–17, were analyzed thematically. Two themes emerged: expectations of evolving responsibility into adulthood, and anxiety about the future that pushed siblings either into action or avoidance when family support was absent. Latino siblings expressed greater certainty about a future caregiving role, framed as duty; non-Latino siblings were more conflicted between their sibling and a hypothetical future family.
studies.why_it_matters: Siblings are the longest-lasting relationship in most autistic people's lives and the de facto succession plan for care, yet almost nothing is known about how children start forming those expectations — or how culture shapes them.
studies.pitch_angle: The 12-year-old who has already decided her life plan around her brother. Lead on the invisible succession planning happening in children's heads, years before any family conversation. Call Kristin Long at Boston University.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the "sibling cliff" — what happens to autistic adults when parents die, and the millions of adult siblings quietly becoming caregivers without recognition or support. Fits a general-interest features section or a long-form audio outlet.
studies.caveats: Small qualitative sample (N=21); interviews conducted in English only, which may select for more acculturated Latino families; single US region; ethnicity treated as a proxy for cultural values; no autistic siblings' own perspectives included.

studies.title: Autistic students in Hong Kong describe masking as both exhausting and worth it
studies.ns_score_reason: a needed non-Western data point that complicates the masking-is-harmful consensus; only eight participants.
studies.the_study: Eight autistic university and college students in Hong Kong were interviewed in Cantonese and analyzed using interpretative phenomenological analysis. Four themes emerged, including motivated but exhausting attempts to connect, and a delicate internal negotiation between masking and unmasking in which students described masking as costly *and* genuinely valuable depending on context. Students wanted support ranging from concrete skills-building to neurodiversity-informed practice, chosen according to their own preferences.
studies.why_it_matters: Most masking research comes from Western, individualist settings where camouflaging is framed largely as harm; these accounts suggest cultural context changes both the cost-benefit calculation and what autistic people actually want from support.
studies.pitch_angle: The neurodiversity movement's strong line on masking meets a collectivist culture where fitting in is not experienced purely as loss. Open with a student weighing when to drop the act. Call Gary Yu Hin Lam at the Chinese University of Hong Kong.
studies.wider_angle: A feature on the cultural provincialism of autism science — how a research literature built on English-speaking Western samples exports assumptions about eye contact, disclosure and authenticity worldwide. Fits a global health or social science outlet.
studies.caveats: Very small qualitative sample (N=8); self-selected, academically successful students only; interpretative analysis is not designed to generalize; no comparison with a Western sample within the same study.

studies.title: Families in Brazil and Spain are still not talking to autistic teens about sex
studies.ns_score_reason: an important, badly neglected topic with a cross-country design, but qualitative and caregiver-only.
studies.the_study: Nineteen primary caregivers of autistic children and adolescents in Brazil and Spain, mostly mothers, gave in-depth interviews about communicating with their children about sexuality, analyzed thematically within Bronfenbrenner's bioecological framework. Two syntheses emerged: family silence born of taboo, trauma and lack of knowledge; and a pattern of daily improvisation, avoided topics and near-absent institutional support from schools and health services.
studies.why_it_matters: Autistic young people face elevated risks of sexual abuse and exploitation and often receive less sex education than peers; this documents the mechanism — not refusal, but silence plus improvisation plus institutional absence — across two very different countries.
studies.pitch_angle: The conversation nobody is having. Lead on a mother improvising an explanation of puberty with no guidance from school or clinician, and the two-country finding that the silence is not culturally specific. Call Talita Gianello André or Lucila Castanheira Nascimento at the University of São Paulo, and María Dolores Gil-Llario at Valencia, who works on sexuality education in disability.
studies.wider_angle: A reported piece on sex education for disabled young people — what evidence-based programs exist, why they rarely reach special education, and the safeguarding argument for teaching rather than protecting through ignorance. Fits an education or social affairs outlet.
studies.caveats: Small qualitative sample (N=19); caregivers only, no autistic young people's own accounts; mothers heavily over-represented; mixed in-person and online recruitment across two countries limits comparability; no outcome data.

studies.title: Changing the building, not the resident, may reduce aggression in care settings
studies.ns_score_reason: a genuinely different framing of "challenging behavior," but only 12 studies survived screening.
studies.the_study: A systematic scoping review searched four databases plus grey literature for 1994–2023 studies on how service organization and managerial practice affect aggression toward people and objects among adults with intellectual disability or autistic adults in formal care. Of 4426 references, just 12 met criteria. Narrative synthesis found reduced frequency and severity of aggression associated with enhanced services and revised care pathways, improved provider accountability, staff support, and more homelike physical environments; grouping similar cases together showed no effect.
studies.why_it_matters: Aggression in care settings is overwhelmingly treated as a property of the individual, addressed with individual behavioral plans and medication; this points at the organization and the building instead — though the evidence base turns out to be startlingly thin.
studies.pitch_angle: What if "challenging behavior" is partly a property of the institution? Pair this with the antipsychotic polypharmacy finding above for a two-study package on how services medicate what they might otherwise design out. Call Yuliya Bodryzlova or Anne Crocker at the Institut national de psychiatrie légale Philippe-Pinel.
studies.wider_angle: An architecture-meets-psychiatry feature on how the physical design of care environments — light, noise, privacy, homeliness — shapes behavior, drawing on dementia unit design and psychiatric ward redesign. Fits a design, architecture or built-environment outlet.
studies.caveats: Only 12 studies included, of heterogeneous and largely uncontrolled design; scoping review does not assess study quality or pool effects; English and French only; no cost or implementation data; causal claims not supportable.

studies.title: A 25-minute autism simulation shifts caregivers' attitudes — at least for a moment
studies.ns_score_reason: the immediate effect sizes are large and the setting is novel, but no control group, no follow-up, and simulations are contested by autistic people themselves.
studies.the_study: At four primary health care centers in Ras Al Khaimah, UAE, 101 mothers and female caregivers with no prior autism training or autistic child completed a standardized 25–30 minute session combining a first-person simulation of sensory and social challenges, guided debriefing and myth correction. Scores on social attitudes, knowledge, willingness to be near autistic people and perspective-taking all rose significantly immediately afterward — social attitudes from 37.7 to 48.3, perspective-taking from 22.2 to 28.0. The authors are explicit that the design cannot establish causality, durability, or an effect of the simulation component alone.
studies.why_it_matters: Stigma-reduction evidence comes overwhelmingly from Western student samples; this tests it in community primary care in the Gulf — but the more interesting question is whether simulating autism actually helps, given sustained criticism from autistic advocates that such exercises breed pity rather than understanding.
studies.pitch_angle: Can you understand autism by pretending to have it for 25 minutes? Use the study as a peg for the wider fight over autism simulations, which some autistic researchers argue increase discomfort and social distance rather than reducing it. Call Fatma Magdi Ibrahim at RAK Medical and Health Sciences University, and an autistic researcher who has published critically on simulation exercises.
studies.wider_angle: A features piece on the evidence base for empathy training in general — VR "walk in their shoes" programs for racism, poverty and disability — and how often immediate attitude change fails to survive a week. Fits a social psychology or education-focused outlet.
studies.caveats: One-group pre-post with no control group and no follow-up; outcomes measured immediately after the session, so demand characteristics are a serious concern; multicomponent intervention means the active ingredient is unidentifiable; self-report attitude scales only; N=101 in a single emirate.

feature_pitch_raw:
**The pattern:** A striking number of studies in this batch show long-standing autism "deficits" shrinking, inverting or relocating once the measurement is tightened. Controlling for chronological age largely dissolves selective-imitation and reduced-face-looking differences in autistic toddlers (PMID 42462495); autistic adults generate counterfactuals just as well as neurotypical adults but default to physical rather than human causes (PMID 41578156); autistic children reach comparable perspective-taking answers with larger, more sustained pupil responses, implying they pay more to get there (PMID 41992731); a pre-registered test finds no speech simplification toward a disclosed-autistic listener at all (PMID 42485806); empathy turns out to amplify rather than buffer the emotional cost of social withdrawal (PMID 42670580); and common-variant genetics look near-identical in males and females, questioning the biological story behind the 4:1 sex ratio (PMID 42658390). Diffusion MRI adds the sharpest warning: the same white matter measure predicts better reading in autistic children and worse reading in neurotypical children (PMID 42619183).

**Why pitch this now:** Autism research is being pushed toward biomarkers, screening tools and AI-assisted detection at exactly the moment when several of its foundational behavioral findings are turning out to depend on how groups were matched, what was self-reported and which direction the effect was assumed to run. The cluster is unusually well timed because the corrections are arriving from independent labs and different methods — genomics, eye-tracking, pupillometry, pre-registered null results — in the same month.

**Angle:** A reported feature on the quiet methodological reckoning inside autism science: what happens to a diagnostic category, and to the services built on it, when "impaired" repeatedly turns out to mean "differently biased," "spotted later," or "working harder for the same result." Written for a general science audience with a stake in the topic — autistic adults, parents, clinicians — with enough method detail to show why age matching and group-by-brain interactions actually decide what we think we know.

**Potential headlines:**
- Control for age, and autism's classic early deficits start to disappear
- Autistic children got the same answers — their pupils showed what it cost
- The autism traits researchers measured may reveal more about who was looking

**Potential outlets:**
- **New Scientist Features** — the batch is squarely Mind territory but too big for a single news item; a features slot allows the genomics, eye-tracking and pupillometry strands to be braided into one argument.
- **The Transmitter (formerly Spectrum)** — its readership is exactly the autism research community arguing about matching, replication and biomarker validity, and it has form on deficit-versus-difference reframings.
- **Undark** — strong fit for the sceptical, methods-forward version: how a research literature's confounds shape clinical categories and funding priorities.
- **Scientific American** — would run the accessible "same performance, different cost" framing with the effort/masking-burnout implication for autistic readers.

fact_check.raw:
# Fact-Check Report: New Scientist Story Ideas — Autism — September 2026
**Checked:** 2026-09-02 | **Studies reviewed:** 19
**Publication:** New Scientist | **Section:** New Scientist Mind

---

### Study 1: Genetic evidence questions why autism is diagnosed so much more often in boys
**PMID:** 42658390 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues (with two moderate framing problems)

**Issue A. "Not explained by sex" applies only to early-diagnosed autism** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Early- and late-diagnosed autism showed strikingly different genetic association profiles, and these differences were not explained by sex."
- **Abstract says:** "Multiple regression models confirmed that early-specific associations were not confounded by biological sex. Conversely, the correlations between late-diagnosed autism and the sex-stratified autism GWAS were near 1, indicating that late-specific associations may be confounded."
- **Problem:** The digest generalizes a result the authors explicitly split. Only the early-diagnosis associations survived the sex control; the late-diagnosis ones may be confounded by sex. Relatedly, "If the common-variant genetics of autism are essentially the same in males and females" overshoots — the same abstract reports stronger internalizing correlations for female-diagnosed autism, i.e. some sex-linked signal.
- **Suggested fix:** "Early-diagnosed autism showed genetic association profiles that differed from late-diagnosed autism and were not confounded by sex; for late-diagnosed autism, correlations with the sex-stratified GWAS were near 1, so those associations may be sex-confounded. The genetic correlation between male and female autism was high, with few sex-specific associations, though female-diagnosed autism did show stronger genetic correlations with internalizing traits."

**Issue B. Pitch hook depends on a dissociation the paper qualifies** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "the finding that the genetics say she is not a different kind of case because she is female, but because she was spotted late"
- **Abstract says:** "the correlations between late-diagnosed autism and the sex-stratified autism GWAS were near 1, indicating that late-specific associations may be confounded"
- **Problem:** The hook asserts that late diagnosis, not sex, is the meaningful genetic axis — but for the late-diagnosed group specifically, the authors say sex and diagnostic timing could not be disentangled. The exciting version of the result is the one the abstract cautions against.
- **Suggested fix:** "Lead on the finding that timing of diagnosis carves up autism genetics at least as sharply as sex does — while being clear that for late-diagnosed autism the two are statistically entangled, and the authors say so."

**Issue C. 4:1 sex ratio not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "the 4:1 diagnostic sex ratio looks less like biology and more like who gets noticed"
- **Abstract says:** "Autism is a neurodevelopmental disorder with a significant male prevalence bias."
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only; the specific ratio comes from outside the paper and varies by source and ascertainment.
- **Suggested fix:** "the well-documented male bias in autism diagnoses looks less like biology and more like who gets noticed, and when"

**Issue D. "Overturns prior research" label is only half right** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "**Novelty:** Overturns prior research"
- **Abstract says:** "Consistent with prior findings, we identified significantly divergent genetic associations with external traits between early- and late-diagnosed autism subtypes."
- **Problem:** The early/late divergence replicates prior work; only the sex result challenges received wisdom. The label as applied to the whole study is too broad. (On NS fit: 7/10 is defensible for a large-sample genomic analysis, but given the acknowledged confounding of the late-diagnosis result I would score it 6.)
- **Suggested fix:** "**Novelty:** Replicates prior subtype findings; challenges the assumed genetic basis of the male prevalence bias"

---

### Study 2: Told a listener is autistic, people don't simplify their speech after all
**PMID:** 42485806 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Framing is consistent with the abstract — N, mean age, paradigm, the null across all four linguistic domains, and the exploratory MLU/attitudes association all match, and the digest correctly presents the finding as a null rather than evidence that patronizing speech doesn't happen.

---

### Study 3: More empathic autistic children fare worse when they withdraw socially
**PMID:** 42670580 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N (689), age range, 76% male, the instruments, the "social avoidance strongest" ranking, and the direction of the moderation (stronger association at higher empathy; no moderation for shyness) all match. Caveats correctly note the cross-sectional, parent-report design and the concurrent outcome.

---

### Study 4: Treating parents' stress lowers autistic preschoolers' emotional meltdowns
**PMID:** 42665438 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues (two moderate)

**Issue A. Causal headline for a secondary outcome with no untreated control** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Treating parents' stress lowers autistic preschoolers' emotional meltdowns"
- **Abstract says:** "Parent-reported child dysregulation and observed dyadic dysregulation decreased significantly across groups, with reduced parenting stress predicting decreased parent-reported dysregulation."
- **Problem:** Improvement occurred *across both active arms*, so the design cannot attribute the decrease to stress treatment; and the significant predictive link was to *parent-reported* dysregulation only, not to observed child dysregulation, which stayed stable. "Meltdowns" also substitutes a behavioral event for the measured construct (emotion dysregulation). The digest body and caveats get this right; the headline does not.
- **Suggested fix:** "Parents' stress falls, and reported child dysregulation falls with it — but the child's solo regulation doesn't budge"

**Issue B. Mischaracterizes what the intervention targeted** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Neither the parents' mental health nor the child was the direct target of child treatment"
- **Abstract says:** "we examined secondary outcomes of a randomized trial ... to assess downstream effects of parent stress-reduction interventions (MBSR vs. Psychoeducational Support) on emotion dysregulation"
- **Problem:** The interventions did directly target parent stress/mental health; the child was the untargeted party. As written the sentence is garbled and contradicts the trial design.
- **Suggested fix:** "The interventions targeted parenting stress, not the child, yet parent-reported child emotion dysregulation and observed dyadic dysregulation both fell across groups."

---

### Study 5: One in five autistic adolescents shows signs of catatonia — most often girls
**PMID:** 42610640 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues (one moderate)

**Issue A. "Most often girls" misstates a predictor as a majority** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "One in five autistic adolescents shows signs of catatonia — most often girls"
- **Abstract says:** "Logistic regression revealed that female gender and clinically significant separation anxiety symptoms were independent predictors of catatonia."
- **Problem:** Female sex raised the odds of catatonia; the abstract never reports the sex composition of the catatonia group. In a male-skewed autism clinic sample the absolute majority of catatonia cases may well have been boys. "Most often girls" states something the data in the abstract do not support.
- **Suggested fix:** "One in five autistic adolescents at a specialist clinic showed signs of catatonia — and girls were at higher risk"

**Issue B. Headline prevalence stated as a general fact** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "One in five autistic adolescents shows signs of catatonia"
- **Abstract says:** "A total of 107 adolescents aged 12-20 years with ASD were evaluated at a tertiary child and adolescent psychiatry outpatient clinic ... Catatonia was identified in 21.5% of participants."
- **Problem:** The caveats flag referral bias, but the headline reads as a population prevalence. Adding two words fixes it.
- **Suggested fix:** See fix in Issue A ("at a specialist clinic").

**Issue C. "Untreatable label" is editorializing hype** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "a treatable condition hiding inside an untreatable label"
- **Abstract says:** "Early recognition and intervention may mitigate functional deterioration and improve clinical outcomes."
- **Problem:** The abstract makes no claim about autism being untreatable, and the phrase imports a contested framing (autism as something to be treated) that New Scientist Mind readers and autistic sources will push back on.
- **Suggested fix:** "a potentially treatable syndrome whose signs are easily read as part of the autism itself"

---

### Study 6: Feeling at home in your body predicts later self-esteem in autistic adults
**PMID:** 42566953 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N (262), age range and mean, 3-month follow-up, the cross-lagged design, the unidirectional effects on self-esteem and flourishing, and the null for life satisfaction all match. "Predicts" is appropriately non-causal, and the intervention-target line mirrors the authors' own hedged wording.

---

### Study 7: A quarter of people with intellectual disability on multiple antipsychotics exceed the maximum recommended dose
**PMID:** 42670819 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues (one moderate)

**Issue A. Omits that most of the cohort had a recorded psychotic illness** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "Autism was recorded in 42–58% of cases and 'behaviours that challenge' in 77–87%."
- **Abstract says:** "Autism (42%-58%), psychotic illness (61%-71%), and behaviours that challenge (77%-87%) were the most common comorbidities."
- **Problem:** The digest selects two of three listed comorbidities and drops the one that most complicates the framing. With psychotic illness recorded in 61–71%, much of this prescribing may be for a licensed indication, which undercuts reading the >1000 mg figure purely as evidence of over-medication for behavior. The abstract also notes higher chlorpromazine-equivalent doses in those with psychosis.
- **Suggested fix:** "Autism was recorded in 42–58% of cases, psychotic illness in 61–71% and 'behaviours that challenge' in 77–87% — and doses were significantly higher in those with psychosis or behaviours that challenge."

**Issue B. Wrong institution for a named source** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Call Rohit Shankar (Cornell/Plymouth)"
- **Abstract says:** "University of Plymouth, UK ... CIDER, Cornwall Partnership NHS Foundation Trust Truro, UK"
- **Problem:** Cornwall, not Cornell. A writer cold-calling on this would look careless.
- **Suggested fix:** "Call Rohit Shankar (University of Plymouth / Cornwall Partnership NHS Foundation Trust)"

---

### Study 8: Autistic adults imagining "what if" blame circumstances where others blame people
**PMID:** 41578156 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Pitch angle turns a difference in degree into a reversal** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "reach for physical rather than human causes"
- **Abstract says:** "while both groups showed a strong preference to produce and fixate human causes, this bias was stronger among neurotypical adults than autistic participants, who more often considered physical causes"
- **Problem:** Both groups preferred human causes; autistic adults just did so less strongly. The caveats acknowledge this ("group difference is in bias strength, not presence"), but the pitch line — and the headline's "blame circumstances where others blame people" — reads as an opposite default, which is the more exciting result a reader would wrongly infer.
- **Suggested fix:** "reach for human causes less reliably, and consider physical ones more often, than neurotypical adults do"

---

### Study 9: Autistic traits show up in how steadily you walk across campus
**PMID:** 41641757 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N (93), the two-trial ignore/attend design, the local/global distinction, the main effect for ASD traits independent of task context, and the explicitly exploratory status of the SAD/ASD context findings all match. The digest is appropriately firm that this is subclinical trait variation, not a diagnostic test.

---

### Study 10: Scrolling without posting is linked to withdrawal in autistic and ADHD young adults
**PMID:** 42430259 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N (101), group sizes, age band, HQ-25M, the null on total online time, the higher hikikomori vulnerability in autistic versus ADHD participants driven by socialization difficulties and physical isolation, and the passive-versus-active association with the Isolation and Emotional Support dimensions all match. The pitch angle explicitly flags unresolved causal direction, which is the right call for cross-sectional self-report.

---

### Study 11: Autistic children's pupils reveal the extra effort of seeing things from another viewpoint
**PMID:** 41992731 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues (one moderate)

**Issue A. "Similar answers by working harder" contradicts the accuracy finding** — Severity: Moderate

- **As written:** "autistic children may reach similar answers by working harder" and, in the wider angle, "why matched task performance can conceal wildly different internal costs"
- **Abstract says:** "Autistic participants showed reduced accuracy when rating an avatar's perspective ... Incongruency elicited stronger effects on behavioral performance and LFSW in autistic relative to neurotypical participants."
- **Problem:** Performance was *not* matched — autistic participants were less accurate and more disrupted by incongruency. The compensation-at-equal-performance story is a different, more appealing result than the one reported. The pupillometry supports greater effort, but alongside poorer performance, not despite equal performance.
- **Suggested fix:** "It suggests that difficulty taking someone else's visual perspective in autism is partly a domain-general problem with filtering out irrelevant information — and that autistic children appear to expend more cognitive effort even while performing less accurately." (And in the wider angle, drop "matched task performance" in favor of "why effort and outcome can come apart.")

---

### Study 12: Control for age, and autistic children's imitation looks much like everyone else's
**PMID:** 42462495 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. The two-study structure, cognitive-age matching with chronological age statistically controlled, multiple-comparison correction, the single surviving group difference on the social door-closed task, the wearable eye-tracking results, and the disappearance of face-directed attention differences after age control all match. Caveats correctly note that sample sizes are absent from the abstract and that statistical control is not design matching.

---

### Study 13: Autistic children's brains take a different route to reading
**PMID:** 42619183 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N (13 vs 12), 16 tracts, higher QA in six tracts and higher isotropic diffusion in two, and the reversed QA–reading comprehension relationship in the left arcuate fasciculus all match. "If it holds" appropriately hedges, and the caveats correctly note that the abstract's own biomarker language outruns the sample size.

---

### Study 14: Parents with depression stick with online parenting therapy best
**PMID:** 42660578 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N (68 dyads), age range, I-PCIT, the ADHD and receptive-language completion predictors, the depression finding (highest completion, greatest improvement in parenting practices), and the ASD result (lesser improvement on one parent-reported measure only, not observed outcomes) all match. Framing stays at the level of prediction within a single treatment cohort, as the caveats state.

---

### Study 15: Latino teenagers assume they'll care for an autistic sibling; others aren't so sure
**PMID:** 42537268 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. "Teenagers" narrows an 8–17 sample** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Latino teenagers assume they'll care for an autistic sibling"
- **Abstract says:** "a non-autistic sibling between 8 and 17 years old"
- **Problem:** Roughly half the eligible age range is pre-teen, and the pitch angle itself opens on a 12-year-old. Calling them all teenagers misstates the population and, given N=21, could mean very few participants were teenagers at all.
- **Suggested fix:** "Latino children and teenagers assume they'll care for an autistic sibling; others aren't so sure"

---

### Study 16: Autistic students in Hong Kong describe masking as both exhausting and worth it
**PMID:** 42522543 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. N (8), Hong Kong postsecondary students, Cantonese interviews, interpretative phenomenological analysis, the four themes including the masking/unmasking negotiation and the preference for support ranging from skills-building to neurodiversity-informed practice all match. The digest is explicit that N=8 and that IPA is not designed to generalize.

---

### Study 17: Families in Brazil and Spain are still not talking to autistic teens about sex
**PMID:** 42528308 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Risk and sex-education claims are not in the abstract** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Autistic young people face elevated risks of sexual abuse and exploitation and often receive less sex education than peers"
- **Abstract says:** Nothing about abuse risk or comparative sex-education receipt; it describes taboo, silence, misinformation and "limited institutional support."
- **Problem:** Unverifiable from abstract only. The claim may be well supported in the wider literature, but as the load-bearing first clause of "Why it matters" it needs its own citation rather than resting on this paper.
- **Suggested fix:** "Sexuality is rarely discussed with autistic young people, and this study documents the mechanism — not refusal, but silence plus improvisation plus institutional absence — across two very different countries. (Source separately for any claim about elevated abuse risk.)"

---

### Study 18: Changing the building, not the resident, may reduce aggression in care settings
**PMID:** 42605201 | **Verdict:** ⚠️ Minor issues

**Issue A. Headline promotes one of four positive intervention categories** — Severity: Minor

- **As written:** "Changing the building, not the resident, may reduce aggression in care settings"
- **Abstract says:** "The following interventions demonstrated positive effects ... enhanced services and revised care pathways, improved provider accountability, staff support and more livable, homelike physical environments."
- **Problem:** Physical environment was one of four categories, and the review does not rank them or pool effects. The headline reads as though building design were the primary finding; the body text is accurate, so this is a headline-emphasis problem.
- **Suggested fix:** "Changing the service, not the resident, may reduce aggression in care settings"

---

### Study 19: A 25-minute autism simulation shifts caregivers' attitudes — at least for a moment
**PMID:** 42556204 | **Verdict:** ✅ Accurate

No factual errors found. Setting (four primary health-care centers, Ras Al Khaimah), N (101), eligibility exclusions, session length and components, the four improved outcomes with p < .001, and the two quoted score changes (37.7→48.3; 22.2→28.0) all match. The digest reproduces the authors' own disclaimer about causality and durability, and the caveats cover the absent control group and follow-up. The "willingness to be near autistic people" gloss for the Personal Distance subscale is a fair rendering.

---
